problem: The conclusion 'sharing only helps when cores have unequal test times' is wrong. For cores tested in parallel over a TAM of fixed width w, the best balanced split gives total time max(T_i/w_i) ≥ (Σ P_i L_i)/w, which is exactly the serial time at full width. So splitting the TAM never beats running the cores one after the other at full width purely on time; the example's own numbers (200,000 = 200,000) show this. What really makes parallel sharing pay off is a core that cannot use the extra width because its internal scan chains are fewer than w, plus power limits that stop all cores running at once.
fix: Step 3: sharing never shortens total time by itself — for these two equal cores, 200,000 cycles in parallel equals 100,000 + 100,000 serial. Sharing pays only when a core cannot use the full width (it has fewer internal scan chains, so extra TAM bits are wasted) or when a power budget forbids testing all cores together. Then parallel testing with a balanced split beats serial testing.
